target: Ten cuidado con el escalón.
english: Be careful with the step.
tip: Ten isn't a typo for tiene – a few common verbs chop the tú command to one syllable: ten, pon, sal. Ten cuidado is literally 'have care'.

target: Sé paciente, ya casi estamos.
english: Be patient, we're almost there.
tip: Sé here means 'be!' – and it's spelled exactly like sé 'I know'. Context decides which; the accent only exists to separate both from the pronoun se.

target: Di la verdad, ¿fuiste tú?
english: Tell the truth, was it you?
tip: Di wears two hats: the command 'tell!' from decir, and 'I gave', the past of dar. Di la verdad commands; ayer di las gracias reports. Context decides.

target: Prueba este plato; está delicioso.
english: Try this dish – it's delicious.
tip: Why está delicioso, not es? Taste is a right-now verdict: está reports how the dish hits your tongue tonight. Es delicioso would rate the recipe in general.

target: Para ser marzo, hace bastante calor.
english: For March, it's quite warm.
tip: Para ser marzo = 'considering it's March'. Para + ser sets a benchmark to judge against – the calor is only remarkable by March standards.

target: Tengo hambre, vamos a comer algo.
english: I'm hungry, let's eat something.
tip: You don't 'be' hungry in Spanish – you have it: tengo hambre, literally 'I have hunger'. Same club: tengo sed, tengo frío, tengo miedo (thirst, cold, fear).

target: Habrá tiempo libre por la tarde.
english: There will be free time in the afternoon.
tip: Habrá is hay sent to the future – and like hay, it never pluralizes: habrá tiempo, habrá problemas. One frozen singular form, however many things will exist.

target: Si mi hijo no estuviera enfermo, iría al colegio.
english: If my son weren't sick, he'd go to school.
tip: English sneaks 'would' into if-clauses; Spanish never does. After si it's estuviera, never estaría – past subjunctive in the if, conditional (iría) in the result.

target: El profesor, cuya clase es difícil, es muy bueno.
english: The teacher, whose class is hard, is very good.
tip: Cuya agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: the male profesor still gets cuya because clase is feminine. English 'whose' never changes shape.

target: El jabón se ha acabado, ¿puedes poner uno nuevo?
english: The soap has run out, can you put a new one?
tip: Nobody used up the soap – it just ended: se ha acabado. That se makes it happen by itself, Spanish's built-in no-blame move for empty jars and dead batteries.

target: Pedí un préstamo al banco para comprar un carro nuevo.
english: I took out a loan from the bank to buy a new car.
tip: Carro is a car in Mexico and most of Latin America – in Spain it's a cart, and Spaniards drive a coche. The same préstamo would buy very different wheels in Madrid.

target: No sé dónde estará, le he llamado y no contesta.
english: I don't know where he could be, I've called and he's not answering.
tip: Estará isn't a prediction here – Spanish uses the future tense for guesses: dónde estará = 'where can he possibly be?' Wondering aloud, not forecasting.

target: De no haber sido por tu ayuda, no lo habria conseguido.
english: Had it not been for your help, I wouldn't have made it.
tip: No si in sight: de no haber sido por = 'had it not been for'. De + infinitive squeezes a whole if-clause into a phrase with no conjugated verb – compact, formal, very written-Spanish.

target: Pregunta por María cuando llegues.
english: Ask for María when you arrive.
tip: Pregunta por María doesn't order her like a menu item – preguntar por means asking after someone. Requesting things is pedir; people take preguntar por.

target: Me gustaría viajar a Japón.
english: I would like to travel to Japan.
tip: "Me gustaría" = I would like. Conditional of gustar for polite wishes. More polite than "quiero."

target: Venid con nosotros a la excursión.
english: Come with us on the excursion.
tip: That -id ending marks the vosotros command, Spain's informal plural: venid = 'come, you all'. Latin America skips vosotros and would say vengan instead.

target: Vamos a pedir unas tapas para compartir.
english: Let's order some tapas to share.
tip: Vamos a pedir can mean 'we're going to order' – but launching a sentence with it usually means 'let's order!' Same phrase covers both plans and proposals.

target: ¿Le importaría hablar un poco más bajo?
english: Would you mind speaking a little quieter?
tip: ¿Le importaría...? literally asks 'would it matter to you?' – Spanish's white-glove request, a notch above ¿podría? Use it on strangers you're about to inconvenience.

target: Cuando seas mayor, entenderás por qué lo hacemos.
english: When you're older, you'll understand why we do it.
tip: 'When you're older' feels like fact in English; Spanish treats unarrived time as unreal: cuando seas, not cuando eres. Future-pointing cuando takes subjunctive.

target: Nos encontramos en la cafetería.
english: We met at the café.
tip: Two 'meets' in Spanish: nos encontramos = we met up (a rendezvous – from encontrar, 'find'); conocer is only for meeting someone for the first time.

target: ¿Le importaría esperar un momento?
english: Would you mind waiting a moment?
tip: "¿Le importaría...?" = Would you mind...? Very formal polite request using conditional of importar.

target: ¿Te importaría revisar mi presentación?
english: Would you mind reviewing my presentation?
tip: Careful answering ¿Te importaría...?: it literally asks 'would it bother you?', so sí = 'yes, I'd mind' – a refusal! To agree to revisar, say claro or no, en absoluto.

target: ¿Quién será a esta hora?
english: Who could that be at this hour?
tip: No one's predicting the future here: Spanish future tense doubles as wondering aloud. ¿Quién será? = 'I wonder who that is' – será guesses, it doesn't forecast.

target: Cuando los niños crezcan, entenderán.
english: When the kids grow up, they'll understand.
tip: English uses plain present for future 'when' (when they grow up); Spanish flags the not-yet-real with subjunctive: cuando crezcan, never cuando crecen.

target: Quería que supieras la verdad.
english: I wanted you to know the truth.
tip: Quería que + imperfect subjunctive: "Quería que lo supieras" (I wanted you to know). Past main clause + que → imperfect subjunctive.

target: Recibí tu mensaje pero no pude contestar.
english: I got your message but I couldn't answer.
tip: No pude isn't just 'couldn't' – the preterite means you hit the wall in that moment: I tried to answer and failed. Ongoing inability would be no podía.

target: Yo que tú no aceptaría esa oferta.
english: If I were you, I wouldn't accept that offer.
tip: Yo que tú is literally 'I that you' – a whole if-I-were-you clause squeezed into three words. It always fires the conditional: no aceptaría.

target: Las personas con las que trabajo son geniales.
english: The people I work with are great.
tip: English strands prepositions ('the people I work with'); Spanish forbids it. Con moves up front and que takes an article: las personas con las que trabajo.

target: Me siento avergonzado por lo que dije ayer.
english: I feel embarrassed about what I said yesterday.
tip: Never translate 'embarrassed' as embarazada – that means pregnant! The safe word is the one this card uses: avergonzado, from vergüenza (shame).

target: El tema del que hablamos ayer es importante.
english: The topic we talked about yesterday is important.
tip: "Del que" = of/about which: "El tema del que hablamos." Contraction of de + el + que.
